title: Get a load of Excel’s new multi-value cells
summary: Until now, Microsoft Excel has followed a strict structural rule: each cell on a worksheet can hold only a single scalar value. While you can string together text using commas or write dynamic array formulas to spill values across adjacent rows and columns, the cell itself remains a single-item container. But Excel has evolved. A feature currently in preview lets you store multiple distinct, structured values within a single cell. Three new data structures can now be put inside a cell: A list maintains a sequence of independent values arranged in a single column. Unlike a plain text string separated by commas, an in-cell list treats each entry as a distinct data element. A list cell can hold a mix of text, numbers, dates, and Boolean values while preserving the native data type of each item. An array stores a grid of rows and columns inside one cell. A nested array allows formulas to generate and return arrays inside other arrays. This allows complex outputs to be confined within individual cells instead of trying to spill them across adjacent worksheet rows and columns. These in-cell data structures can simplify complex formula processing and reduce clutter on the worksheet. Availability: These in-cell data structures are available in Excel for Windows and Mac to members of the Microsoft 365 Insider program who are on the Beta Channel. Microsoft has not yet said when the features will begin rolling out to all M365 subscribers, and they are not supported in perpetual license versions (such as Office 2021 or Office 2024) or Excel for the web. Use cases Here are examples of how these three in-cell structures can be used. Multi-item categorizing Imagine categorizing your co-workers, who each have expertise in using up to five M365 software tools: Excel, OneNote, Outlook, PowerPoint, and Word. title: MariaDB enhances agent development for its next-gen database platform
summary: MariaDB on Wednesday said it was adding four new agent-focused capabilities to Enterprise Platform 2027, the latest version of its enterprise database platform, to help developers retrieve enterprise data faster, maintain agent memory across sessions, and reduce the cost and latency of repeated model queries. These new capabilities include AI Retrieval, AI Plugins, Agent Memory, and Semantic Cache. While AI Retrieval is designed to help agents access information from enterprise documents and live operational data through a single managed service, AI Plugins are designed to bring MariaDB-specific expertise into coding agents such as Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex , helping developers generate database-related code more accurately, the company said in a statement. AI Retrieval also converts natural-language questions into read-only SQL queries, which MariaDB said would eliminate the need for developers to manually write queries for every request. Agent Memory, meanwhile, provides agents with a persistent, in-memory store that allows them to retain information across sessions and resume tasks without having to rebuild their context each time, according to the company. Semantic Cache, the fourth capability, is intended to reduce response times and AI inference costs by identifying semantically similar questions, even when phrased differently, and reusing previously generated answers instead of processing each query from scratch, MariaDB said. AI retrieval simplifies data access, but raises reliability concerns For developers, AI Retrieval can increase productivity, said Ashish Chaturvedi , executive research leader at HFS Research. “Most RAG setups keep documents in a vector store and live records in the transactional database, with glue code deciding which to query and how to merge results. title: How will we make senior developers?
summary: Something strange is going on in the job market for software developers. Everyone is worried that their job is going to go away and businesses are going to turn software development over to the machines. Few dispute that agents write good code . I’ve even argued that our days of writing code are pretty much over . Sure, agents are writing the code, but we aren’t quite ready to turn the whole thing over to agents. We are still feeling the need to supervise what they do, look closely at the code they write, and serve as gatekeeper for what gets checked into Git. We can do this because we are seasoned, experienced developers, with hundreds of thousands of lines of code under our belt, and we’ve seen it all. We can spot bad designs, inefficient algorithms, and code smells. If the agent isn’t doing things the right way, we can spot the problem and correct it. Coders of hard knocks And how did we become seasoned, experienced developers? We started out writing bad code that was reviewed — probably first by a high school teacher or college professor, and later by senior devs. Or maybe we just wrote a lot of sloppy code and learned it was sloppy by reading, studying, and gaining experience on our own. But however it happened, it was more or less “learn by doing.” But we aren’t “doing” anymore. So the question becomes, how is anyone going to learn to code if we don’t code? It doesn’t take advanced calculus to realize that if we don’t teach early-career developers how to develop software, then we will lose all the expertise in the profession as time relentlessly marches forward. The classic example of a job that AI promised to take was radiology. The thinking was that AI can look at an x-ray and see the problems as well as or better than any human — often spotting problems that humans would overlook. These behaviors let you take web pages that already use JavaScript, and either migrate to htmx entirely or add htmx only where it’s needed — for instance, in new parts of an application. Generally, htmx works best with green-field applications, since you can start with a non-interactive page and just layer in the behaviors you want as they’re needed. But htmx can also work as an add-on for a page that already uses JavaScript, or as a migration target away from existing JavaScript. Using htmx with JavaScript When you want to integrate htmx with hand-rolled JavaScript, htmx offers you several ways to do it. Some are extremely basic, but tightly coupled to the objects they work with. Others are more advanced and flexible, but require more work to use. Using hx-on attributes A basic way to add JavaScript behaviors to objects is through a very htmx-like mechanism, the hx-on attributes. Add one of these to a given object and you can provide code or function calls inline. For example: Click here to log to the console The inline code can be a whole code block, as shown here, or a function call to your own code. One advantage of using hx-on is consistency with other hx- attributes. If all your existing interaction is powered by htmx, adding more hx- attributes for custom functionality keeps things uniform. On the other hand, if you want your custom functionality to be mechanically distinct from htmx, consider the approach discussed next: registering callbacks. Using the htmx API The more complex way to “wire up” JavaScript functionality for htmx-enabled pages is to use the htmx object and its methods. summary: Release: datasette-apps 0.3a0 Datasette Apps adds support for hosting and editing custom HTML applications inside of Datasette. These can be created by hand, but it's easier to create them using LLMs via Datasette Agent . This release improves that integration: Apps can now be tagged in Datasette Agent chat messages by typing # , which autocompletes from the apps the user has permission to view. New app_add_stored_queries() and app_remove_stored_queries() tools let the agent manage which stored queries an app is allowed to call. Granting a write query requires approval from the user first. app_create() now checks that each requested stored query exists and that the user can view it, and asks the user to approve any write queries before the app is created. The "View app" buttons shown by the agent tools, and the links on # app references, now open the app full screen in the Datasette Agent panel. Tags: datasette , datasette-agent , datasette-apps
